cases.goal: Examine the provided NYC trajectory records and explain the main regularities and deviations in the observed mobility behavior.

insights.insight: Car trips have a higher median observed speed than walking trips, while walking trips have a higher median route-indirectness score in the selected records.
A small number of trajectories deviate from the usual speed and distance patterns of the collection.
Some trajectories that deviate from the normal speed and distance ranges contain isolated GPS points that drift outside their main trajectory paths, possibly because of positioning errors.

cases.summary: The records show a clear mode-associated difference in both speed and route indirectness, together with a small number of trajectories that deviate from the usual speed and distance patterns. The revised drift view compares observed GPS positions with WorldTrace per-point matching references and shows where the point-to-reference offsets become unusually large; the reference markers are not a connected road map.

cases.goal: Analyze the provided trajectory histories to compare observed mode composition, repeated spatial use, and driving-speed behaviour across three users.

insights.insight: Within the provided histories, user_01 and user_02 prefer driving rather than walking, while user_03 has no obvious preference because the observed car and walking counts are balanced.

Across all provided driving trajectories, the three users pass through the same South Brooklyn area and their paths overlap along the same road corridor; the walking paths are shown separately rather than being used to support the driving-road claim.

The three users show clearly different driving-speed behaviour: user_01 drives faster and with larger within-trip speed variation, whereas user_02 and user_03 drive at lower, comparatively stable speeds.

cases.summary: Within the provided histories, user_01 and user_02 prefer driving rather than walking while user_03 has no obvious preference. Across all provided driving trajectories, the three users pass through the same local South Brooklyn area and shared road corridor. Their driving speeds separate into a higher, more variable profile for user_01 versus stable lower-speed profiles for user_02 and user_03.

insights.insight: wt03_trajectory_22 and wt03_trajectory_23 differ from the typical patterns: their average speeds are much higher, while wt03_trajectory_24 differs from the others because the traveled distance is the longest and much longer than the others.

cases.goal: Identify movement groups among the provided trajectories based on their regions and analyze the resulting groups.

insights.insight: The provided trajectories form four equally sized start-region groups: Brooklyn, Manhattan, NJ side, and Queens each contribute 12 trajectories.

The geographic groups differ in their observed distance and route-indirectness summaries: NJ side and Queens have the largest median distances; NJ side has the highest median route-indirectness score; and Brooklyn has both the lowest average distance and the most direct routes.
In the Brooklyn group, most trajectories are walking trips, making it the only walking-dominant group; its average trajectory distance is also much shorter than that of the other groups.

cases.summary: The provided trajectories form four equally sized regional groups. NJ side and Queens have the largest median distances, NJ side has the highest median route indirectness, and Brooklyn combines the shortest average distance with the most direct routes. Brooklyn is also the only walking-dominant group, so movement mode remains part of the regional comparison.

cases.goal: Analyze the provided trajectories within a common area and identify how their movement characteristics vary across time periods.

insights.insight: On cold days, more vehicle trajectories pass through the South Brooklyn area during daytime hours than during non-daytime hours.
Afternoon trajectories usually have higher route-indirectness scores than trajectories in the other time periods.
Trajectories in the morning and around midnight have much higher average speeds than trajectories in the other time periods.

cases.summary: Across 64 vehicle trajectories in the same South Brooklyn area over four consecutive days, cold-day vehicle trajectories are more numerous during daytime hours, afternoon trajectories have the highest route-indirectness scores, and morning and midnight trajectories have the highest average speeds.

cases.goal: Analyze the provided user's normal movement pattern and identify anomalous trajectories.

insights.insight: The user repeatedly travels between Area A and Area B: 36 of 40 trajectories, or 90%, belong to this bidirectional corridor, with 18 trips in each direction.
When driving between Area A and Area B, the user takes multiple route corridors, and traveled distances vary widely across these trips.
Outside the main Area A–Area B corridor, the remaining four trajectories are evenly distributed across four regions, with one trajectory in each region.
The user's driving speeds are tightly clustered within a narrow range across both the main corridor and the other regional trips, including the less urban regional routes.
Exactly one trajectory is a route-shape anomaly: it forms a loop and starts and ends at the same geographic point, unlike the other trajectories.

cases.summary: The user exhibits a strong bidirectional Area A–Area B corridor pattern: 36 of 40 trajectories belong to it, although the trips use multiple route corridors and have a wide distance range. The four remaining trajectories are evenly distributed across four regions. Driving speeds stay tightly clustered across both the main corridor and the other regional trips. One trajectory is a unique geometric exception because it forms a closed loop and returns to its starting point.

cases.goal: Investigate how weather conditions are associated with changes in the user's usual travel behavior.

insights.insight: In the observed records, rainy and snowy conditions coincide with lower average speeds and smaller mean yaw changes than dry conditions.
On cold rainy days, the user's trajectories are shorter on average than on dry days with normal temperatures.
During cold rainy conditions, car trajectories outnumber walking trajectories. Several very short car trajectories lower the average distance, although a few car trajectories remain long.
On very hot days above 35°C, the user generates only a few trajectories across both car and walking modes.
The few car trajectories recorded above 35°C are more direct, with lower route-indirectness scores than the user's normal car trajectories.

cases.summary: The user's observed travel behavior varies across weather conditions: rainy and snowy records have lower speeds and smaller yaw changes, cold rainy trips are shorter and dominated by car travel, very hot days contain few trajectories in either mode, and the few hot-weather car trips are more direct than normal car trips.

cases.goal: Analyze how the traveler selects routes across repeated trips and identify the trade-offs that appear to shape their route choices.

insights.insight: Although Route A is not always the fastest option, the traveler repeatedly chooses it across similar trips, and its travel time varies substantially less than the alternatives.
Most trips follow the same familiar corridor, but this journey switches to a different route midway and reconnects with the habitual route near the destination.
The selected route is longer than the shorter alternative, but it maintains higher and more stable speeds for most of the trip, resulting in a comparable overall travel time.

cases.summary: Across similar trips, Route A is the most frequent and most predictable choice even though alternatives can be faster. One trip temporarily leaves the habitual corridor, and the detailed comparison shows how a longer but faster and steadier route can match the travel time of a shorter alternative.

cases.goal: Identify the major changes in movement behavior during the trip and detect abnormal movement segments.

insights.insight: The strongest speed reductions consistently occur around the sharpest bends in the route, while movement remains relatively stable along straight road sections.
The trip remains direct for most of the journey but becomes slow and locally circuitous near the destination, where repeated turns account for most of the excess travel distance.
A prolonged low-speed segment appears in the middle of the trip despite relatively smooth movement before and after it, making this section the primary disruption to an otherwise stable journey.

cases.summary: The journey is mostly stable and direct, but three movement changes stand out: brief speed reductions at sharp bends, a prolonged low-speed disruption in the middle, and a slow, repeatedly turning destination phase where most excess distance accumulates.

cases.goal: Summarize the commuting driving behavior of users from the supplied repeated travel trajectories.

insights.insight: Although users repeatedly commute between Northgate Residential District and Harbor Business District in both directions, most retain one fixed route; only 25% ever switch between corridors for the same origin–destination pair.

Despite user-level route variation, a clear main corridor is used by most trips, and the full time intervals spent on it consistently remain within the 07:00–10:00 morning and 16:00–18:00 afternoon commuting periods.
Among the 25% of users who try alternatives, alternative-route use declines over repeated commutes; after the fifth commute, all of them use the main commuting corridor.

cases.summary: Most users repeatedly drive the same corridor between the two commuting districts, while only three users initially explore alternatives. The main corridor dominates the supplied trips, with each complete traversal remaining in the morning or afternoon commuting windows. The users who explored alternatives converge to the main corridor after several repeated commutes.

Return visits are concentrated disproportionately on locations that have already been visited frequently.

cases.summary: Most observed visits return to previously visited areas, while only a smaller share expands the user's visited-location set. cases.goal: Identify the directional, temporal, and mode patterns in the user's trajectories.

insights.insight: The user's trajectories are strongly concentrated along a limited set of movement directions rather than being distributed uniformly around the activity space.
The concentrated movement directions are not dominant in evening times across different days.

The user shows preference of driving rather than walking or cycling for the concentrated movement directions while other routes are used less frequently, and a higher mean speed can be observed in the concentrated route.

cases.goal: Analyze vehicle use and associated trajectory characteristics across the supplied travel history.

insights.insight: Large-vehicle trips tend to follow longer trajectories with higher route directness, while smaller vehicles use a wider variety of shorter and more turning-intensive routes.
Large vehicles maintain more stable speeds along their trajectories, whereas smaller vehicles show greater within-trip speed variation, particularly on routes with frequent directional changes.
GPS positions from large-vehicle trips are more consistently aligned with matched roads, while some small-vehicle trajectories contain larger point-to-road offsets in locally complex route segments.
Higher temperature is associated with more frequent use of smaller vehicles, while lower temperature is associated with more frequent use of larger vehicles.

cases.goal: Investigate changes in travel behavior and movement conditions under varying environmental conditions.

Although car travel becomes more dominant during poor weather, the car trajectories in such cases are concentrated in relatively shorter-distance movements and do not increase the overall spatial extent of mobility.
